CONNECTING THE WORLD

Jet airliner.

Speed, altitude, and a cabin built for people. Jet airliners make journeys between cities and continents part of everyday life.

OverviewKey featuresHow it worksCommon usesQuestions
01 / THE BIG PICTURE

Meet the jet airliner.

A jet airliner is a powered, fixed-wing aircraft designed to transport passengers. Its shape balances aerodynamic efficiency, cabin space, and the demands of repeated airport operations.

SPOT IT IN THE SKY

Look for a long cabin with rows of windows, swept wings, large engine nacelles, and retractable landing gear.

02 / DESIGN DETAILS

What makes it different.

01

Swept wings

On many airliners, rearward-swept wings help manage airflow at high cruising speeds.

02

Pressurized cabin

A controlled cabin environment lets passengers travel at altitudes where outside air pressure is much lower.

03

Retractable landing gear

The wheels retract after takeoff to reduce aerodynamic drag.

04

High-lift devices

Flaps and slats change the wing’s shape during slower phases such as takeoff and landing.

03 / HOW IT WORKS

The engineering
behind the flight.

Turbofan engines accelerate air backward to produce forward thrust. As the airplane moves, airflow around the wings generates lift. Pilots and flight-control systems adjust control surfaces to manage pitch, roll, and yaw. In a steady, level cruise, lift balances weight and thrust balances drag.

04 / IN THE REAL WORLD

Made for a mission.

  • Scheduled passenger services between cities
  • Long-distance and intercontinental travel
  • Charter flights and group transport
CAPABILITIES & TRADEOFFS

Jet airliners are well suited to moving many passengers over long distances, but need airport infrastructure, trained crews, and extensive maintenance. A smaller aircraft can be a better fit for a short route with few passengers.

05 / A CLOSER LOOK

Good questions.

Do all airliners have two engines?

No. Engine arrangements vary by design. Two-engine layouts are common, while some aircraft use other configurations.

Why do they fly high?

At suitable cruising altitudes, jet airliners can travel efficiently in thinner air. The chosen altitude depends on aircraft weight, weather, traffic, and performance.

This guide describes an aircraft category. Equipment, speed, range, capacity, and operating limitations vary by model and configuration. Categories can overlap: a propeller aircraft can also be a cargo plane or seaplane.
